hints: Start by listing what you are told is formed, iodine ($\text{I}_2$) and white solid copper(I) iodide ($\text{CuI}$), and work out the oxidation number change for copper and iodine.
walkthrough:
Sort out oxidation and reduction**
Think with me. $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ends up as $\text{Cu}^{+}$ in $\text{CuI}$, so each copper gains one electron and is reduced. $\text{I}^{-}$ ends up partly as $\text{I}^{-}$ in $\text{CuI}$ and partly as $\text{I}_{2}$, so some iodide is oxidised to iodine.

Balance to make the ionic equation**
You need $2\text{Cu}^{2+}$ to make $2\text{CuI}$, which needs $2\text{I}^{-}$ for the precipitate plus another $2\text{I}^{-}$ to make $\text{I}_{2}$. That gives: $2\text{Cu}^{2+} + 4\text{I}^{-} \rightarrow 2\text{CuI} + \text{I}_{2}$. Check atoms and charge, both sides balance.

hints: Recall what water ligands do to the five 3d orbitals of a $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ion in $[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$.
Think about what happens when white light shines on that complex and an electron can move between the split d levels.
Link the energy gap between the split d orbitals to a specific frequency or wavelength of light being removed from white light.
Remember that the colour you see is never the colour absorbed, it is what is left over or transmitted.
walkthrough:
Picture the d orbitals splitting**
In solution copper(II) exists as the complex $[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$. On its own the five 3d orbitals have the same energy, but when six water ligands approach, they repel d electrons unequally. This splits the 3d set into two groups with a small energy gap. $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is $3\text{d}^9$, so there is a vacancy in the upper level.

Promote an electron with light energy**
When white light passes through, an electron in the lower 3d level can absorb exactly the energy of the gap and jump up to the higher 3d level. This is called a d-d transition. Only photons with that exact energy, so one particular frequency and wavelength, are absorbed.

Explain the colour you actually see**
White light minus the absorbed wavelength leaves all the other wavelengths to pass through. Your eye sees the mixture of the remaining wavelengths, which is the complementary colour to the colour absorbed. For copper(II) sulfate this appears blue.

Final answer: Ligands cause splitting of 3d orbitals into two energy levels.
An electron is promoted / excited from lower to higher 3d level.
A specific wavelength / frequency of visible light is absorbed to provide this energy.
Colour seen is the complementary colour to that absorbed, i.e. light not absorbed is transmitted / seen.

hints: Write the electron configuration of $\text{Cu}^{+}$ starting from Cu $[\text{Ar}]3\text{d}^{10}4\text{s}^1$ and think whether a d electron has anywhere to move to.
walkthrough:
Check the d shell filling**
Copper atom is $[\text{Ar}]3\text{d}^{10}4\text{s}^1$. Remove the $4\text{s}$ electron and one $3\text{d}$ electron to get $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ($3\text{d}^9$), but remove only the $4\text{s}$ electron to get $\text{Cu}^{+}$ ($3\text{d}^{10}$). In $\text{CuI}$ the copper is $\text{Cu}^{+}$ with a completely full 3d subshell.

Link full shell to white appearance**
Because every 3d orbital is full, there is no vacant higher d level for an electron to be promoted into. No d-d transition can occur, so no wavelength of visible light is absorbed and the solid appears white.
Final answer: $\text{Cu}^{+}$ is $3\text{d}^{10}$, the 3d subshell is full so no d-d electron transition is possible and no visible light is absorbed.

hints: From the Data Booklet pick out the two relevant $E^{\circ}$ values, one for $\text{Cu}^{2+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Cu}^{+}$ and one for $\text{I}_{2} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{I}^{-}$.
Decide which half cell would be reduction and which would be oxidation if $\text{I}^{-}$ reduced $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, then check the sign of $E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{red} - E^{\circ}_{ox}$.
walkthrough:
Pull out the correct standard potentials**
Let me show you how to choose. You need the reduction with $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ going to $\text{Cu}^{+}$: $$\text{Cu}^{2+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Cu}^{+} \quad E^{\circ} = +0.15\ \text{V}$$ And the reduction with iodine going to iodide: $$\text{I}_{2} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{I}^{-} \quad E^{\circ} = +0.54\ \text{V}$$

Test feasibility with Ecell**
If $\text{I}^{-}$ reduced $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, then $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is reduced and $\text{I}^{-}$ is oxidised. So: $$E^{\circ}_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{\text{(reduction)}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{(oxidation)}} = 0.15 - 0.54 = -0.39\ \text{V}$$ A negative $E^{\circ}_{cell}$ means the reaction is not feasible under standard conditions. Put simply, the more positive $E^{\circ}$ wins, so $\text{I}_{2}$ is more easily reduced than $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ to $\text{Cu}^{+}$, and the reverse reaction is favoured.

Final answer: $E^{\circ}(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}^{+}) = +0.15\ \text{V}$ and $E^{\circ}(\text{I}_{2}/\text{I}^{-}) = +0.54\ \text{V}$.
$E^{\circ}_{cell} = 0.15 - 0.54 = -0.39\ \text{V}$, negative so not feasible under standard conditions. $\text{I}_{2}$ is the stronger oxidant and $\text{I}^{-}$ cannot reduce $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ to $\text{Cu}^{+}$.

hints: Focus on the $\text{Cu}^{2+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Cu}^{+}$ equilibrium and ask what removing $\text{Cu}^{+}$ as solid $\text{CuI}$ does to the position of equilibrium.
Recall that removing a product drives reduction forward, making $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ a stronger oxidant, so compare the new non-standard $E$ value with $+0.54\ \text{V}$ for iodine.
walkthrough:
See why standard conditions no longer apply**
Standard $E^{\circ}$ assumes all ions at $1.0\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$. Here $\text{CuI}$ is very insoluble, so as soon as $\text{Cu}^{+}$ forms it precipitates and $[\text{Cu}^{+}]$ drops far below $1.0\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$. For the equilibrium $$\text{Cu}^{2+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Cu}^{+}$$ removing $\text{Cu}^{+}$ pulls the equilibrium to the right by Le Chatelier's principle.

Follow the change in electrode potential**
Driving that reduction forward makes $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ much more keen to gain an electron, so its electrode potential $E$ becomes more positive than the standard $+0.15\ \text{V}$. It rises until it is more positive than $+0.54\ \text{V}$ for $\text{I}_{2}/\text{I}^{-}$. Now $E_{cell}$ is positive, the reaction becomes feasible, and that is why excess $\text{I}^{-}$ does reduce $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ in practice despite the prediction in (c).

Final answer: Precipitation of $\text{CuI}$ lowers $[\text{Cu}^{+}]$ well below $1.0\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$, shifting $\text{Cu}^{2+} + \text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Cu}^{+}$ to the right.
$E(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu}^{+})$ becomes more positive, rising above $E(\text{I}_{2}/\text{I}^{-}) = +0.54\ \text{V}$, so $E_{cell}$ becomes positive and $\text{I}^{-}$ can reduce $\text{Cu}^{2+}$.
